title: ABC Asks Judge to Stop Early Government Review of Its TV Station Licenses
summary:
The TV network ABC asked a federal judge in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday to stop the Trump administration from carrying out an unusual early review of its broadcast licenses.

TV stations need licenses from the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, to use the public airwaves. These licenses are usually renewed on a regular schedule. In April, FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr ordered eight ABC-owned stations to apply for renewal years ahead of time. According to the Associated Press, the order came just after a joke by ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel angered President Donald Trump.

ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC in August. The network says the early review breaks the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment, which protects free speech and a free press. ABC says it is being punished for content the president dislikes.

At a two-hour hearing, ABC lawyer Beth Wilkinson said the review is already affecting the network's news choices as the midterm elections approach. "We are watching everything that we do," she said.

A Justice Department lawyer, Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel, disagreed. He argued that the case belongs in a different court. He also said ABC had not shown real harm, because its eight licenses are still valid. Carr has said broadcasters have a duty to "operate in the public interest."

Judge Loren AliKhan asked both sides many questions but did not rule right away. She asked for more written arguments by Oct. 9 from the government and by Oct. 14 from ABC. A decision is not expected until at least mid-October.

The case is one of several legal fights between the administration and news organizations, including the Associated Press, over news coverage and access to the government.
why_it_matters: The case tests how far the government can go in reviewing a news organization's licenses without limiting free speech. Its outcome could affect other broadcasters, not just ABC.

background_read: The Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, is the U.S. government agency that manages the public airwaves used by TV and radio stations.
Local stations must hold FCC licenses, which are normally renewed on a regular schedule if the station serves the public interest.
The First Amendment to the Constitution protects free speech and a free press, which limits how the government can punish news outlets for what they say.
When a company believes a government action is illegal, it can sue and ask a judge for a preliminary order to pause that action while the case continues.
